Orthodontic pain

Results are mixed; small trials report short-term pain reduction in some treatment settings, but the effect is not consistent.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Results are mixed; small trials report short-term pain reduction in some treatment settings, but the effect is not consistent.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact orthodontic-pain category contains 79 unique titles, including 52 human randomized reports, four nonrandomized human studies, four rat studies, 16 reviews or syntheses, two protocols, and one editorial. Reviews summarize overlapping clinical reports. The pain category is separate from the tooth-movement title category, although outcomes or cohorts may be related. (Dezfully et al. 2026)

Human and clinical evidence

Human randomized trials evaluate pain after separators, archwire placement, activation, or other orthodontic procedures. The 2026 exploratory split-mouth trial in 31 adults found pain differences at 24 hours between three active regimens and placebo, but the highest and lowest scores varied by regimen and outcome. Its retrospective registration and small sample limit confidence. Other studies and reviews report variable short-term effects.

Animal evidence

Four rat studies are indexed. They provide preclinical information about nociception or tissue response but do not establish analgesic benefit in orthodontic patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate in-vitro or ex-vivo publication is identified in the exact category. Reviews and animal experiments remain distinct from human pain outcomes.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2026 study used a 980 nm near-infrared GaAlAs diode at 0.1–0.2 W in a single application. The three regimens delivered 6 J continuous, 12 J continuous, or 6 J pulsed. Other reports use different wavelengths, doses, schedules, and treatment timing, so there is no common protocol for general recommendation.

Interpretation

Evidence suggests possible short-term relief in some orthodontic procedures but does not establish a consistent effect across pain types or follow-up periods. Future trials should preregister, use adequate sample sizes, blind participants and assessors, and report pain at consistent time points together with rescue medication and adverse events.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain relief in selected orthodontic settings
Publications and records79 unique titles in Oral > Orthodontics > Pain.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category includes 79 titles, with many small randomized studies and overlapping reviews. Pain timing, orthodontic procedures, doses, and comparators vary. A recent split-mouth study reported a short-term signal but was exploratory and retrospectively registered. Larger preregistered trials should use standardized pain measures and analgesic-use outcomes.
